RED HERRING 1: SUBTRACTION ISN’T A GROWTH MODEL

• PARCC doesn’t have a vertical scale so subtract isn’t even justified.
• People will subtract even though they aren’t supposed to. The PARCC scale runs
 from 650 to 850 across all content areas and grades.
• Even if you could subtract, the previous example shows that subtracting (and
 then comparing gains) is highly problematic.
• States with vertical scales (e.g., SBAC states) all demonstrate the “high jumper
 phenomenon”: Low achievers gain more than high achievers.

RED HERRING 1: SUBTRACTION ISN’T A GROWTH MODEL

• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student with similar
 characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students with (at
 least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for stakeholders to
 understand student growth.
• Peer based norms are possible even across test transitions like New Jersey’s
 transition from NJASK to PARCC.

RED HERRING 2: DIFFICULT TO CALCULATE SO CAN’T UNDERSTAND

• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and popular
 perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student growth is
 not synonymous with understanding student growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to
 understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to calculate
 but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple conceptual basis.

RED HERRING 3: NOT CAUSAL SO INAPPROPRIATE FOR EVALUATION

• There is active debate about whether it is possible to isolate the the unique
 contribution of a teacher from the data derived from state summative
 assessments like PARCC (i.e., are causal estimates)
• The pro-argument: If they are causal, then it is hard to deny using them for
 evaluation purposes.
• The con-argument: If they aren’t causal, then they shouldn’t be used for
 evaluation purposes.
• The con-argument is a red herring (even if estimates are not causal).
• Society employs numerous non-causal quantities for evaluation purposes (e.g.,
 win/loss percentage, student satisfaction, …).
• In fact, I’m at a loss to come up with a single example where an actual causal
 estimator is used for actual institutional or personnel evaluation.

RESULTS: SGP PROPERTIES

• SGPs are uncorrelated with prior achievement at the student
 level (i.e., a conditional probability)

• SGPs are correlated with current achievement. I.e., higher
 growth is associated with higher achievement and vice-versa.

• SGPs for students are uncorrelated from year to year.

BACKGROUND

• 2016 SGP analyses of New Jersey PARCC data were conducted in September 2016.

• This follows 2015 SGP analyses of New Jersey PARCC data conducted in late 2015/early 2016.

• SGP analyses of New Jersey data have been performed since 2010.

• Analyses were conducted using PARCC theta values (instead of scaled scores) and scale scores
 for NJASK as priors to avoid any potential issues with ceiling/ oor effects.

 • Of the 4 PARCC states we work with on SGP analyses, 3 are using theta values.

 • PARCC SGP analyses are conducted using theta values.

• Results from SGP analyses (only ELA and Mathematics) are used, in part, for educator
 evaluation.
